23 A beam of red laser light has length 1.0 m.
What is the order of magnitude of the number of wavelengths of the red light in 1.0 m?
A
104
B
106
C
108
D
1010

hints: Notice the length to fill is $1.0 \text{ m}$ and you need the typical wavelength of red visible light in $\text{nm}$ or $\text{m}$.
Recall red light is at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum, about $600$-$700 \text{ nm}$, or about $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
Connect the count to $N = L/\lambda$ with $L = 1.0 \text{ m}$, then round the result to the nearest power of 10.
walkthrough: Identify the given length $L = 1.0 \text{ m}$ and recall the wavelength of red laser light is about $650 \text{ nm} \approx 6.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
State the rule for the number of waves in a length: $N = L / \lambda$.
Substitute values with units: $N \approx 1.0 \text{ m} / 6.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{6}$.
Check order of magnitude: $1.5 \times 10^{6}$ is closest to $10^{6}$ rather than $10^{4}$ or $10^{8}$.

A.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 100. It would need a wavelength of about $10^{-4} \text{ m}$, which is infrared, not red light.

B.explanation: Red light has $\lambda \approx 7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, so $N = 1.0/\lambda \approx 1.4 \times 10^{6}$, whose order of magnitude is $10^{6}$.

C.explanation: Too large by a factor of about 100. It would need a wavelength of about $10^{-8} \text{ m}$, which is X-ray, not visible red light.

D.explanation: Far too large. It would need a wavelength of about $10^{-10} \text{ m}$, which is atomic size and gamma-ray region.
